Subject: Connectivity options for HarborBank private stack

Hi Olga,

Thanks for taking this. We’re evaluating Redwood Private (VPC/on-prem) and need a clear recommendation on connectivity patterns. High-level constraints: low-latency calls from our app to model endpoints (regional), scope limited by PCI (no public egress for cardholder data), cross-account replication (primary in us-east-1, DR in us-west-2), and the ability to route traffic from our on-prem data centers for a small subset of services.

Specifically, we want to understand tradeoffs between: VPC Peering, PrivateLink (VPC Endpoint Service), and site-to-site VPN (IPsec). Key questions:
- Which approach gives the best isolation for PCI?
- Expected latency and jitter impacts (ballpark) for small request/response patterns (~200B request, ~1KB response).
- Operational complexity for cross-account DR and on-prem connectivity.
- Any blockers for our plan to keep model inference traffic inside our network and Redwood Private (no public NAT).

Can you share a short matrix and suggest an initial path? Also please loop in any network engineers we should talk to.

Thanks,

Rajiv — thanks, good summary. I put together a short matrix (attached) and a recommended starting architecture after talking to our infra team. High level:

- VPC Peering: lowest intra-region latency (layer 3 routing), simple for same-account or between accounts if you handle route propagation. Downsides: full routability -> larger blast radius, manual route management across many VPCs, not ideal for tightly scoped PCI segmentation unless you pair with strong security groups + NACL strategy. Cross-region peering is possible but adds egress charges and can get complex for DR.

- PrivateLink (VPC Endpoint Service): presents Redwood as a service endpoint in your VPC. Pros: strong control plane and scoped connectivity (only the service port is exposed), works cleanly cross-account, and avoids public IPs. Cons: each PrivateLink ENI has bandwidth limits (per-AZ), potential per-GB charges; extra hop (ENI -> service) but usually small latency penalty. This is often our recommendation where strict isolation and PCI are priorities.

- Site-to-Site VPN (IPsec): fast to stand up and familiar, good for connecting on-prem quickly. Throughput, latency, and jitter depend on your appliance and internet path. For production inference traffic we see VPNs as a fallback or for control/management planes rather than primary low-latency token streams.

Recommendation for HarborBank (initial):
1) Proof-of-concept using PrivateLink into a dedicated Redwood VPC (single-tenant service endpoints) for PCI-scoped inference traffic.
2) Separate replication/replica-sync traffic can use a VPC Peering or Transit Gateway link between your replication VPCs (we can limit routing to only the necessary prefixes).
3) Use S2S VPN only for on-prem connections that can tolerate higher jitter or as a constrained path for secondary workloads.

Attachments: harbor-connectivity-matrix-v1.pdf (matrix + quick diagrams), privatelink-performance-tests.xlsx (our internal baseline numbers).

Next steps: Connor (CC’d) can sketch a CIDR and routing plan and propose a PoC checklist. If OK, I’ll set a 45-minute technical call next week with your NetOps and our infra.

Rajiv / Olga — quick technical follow-up from infra after reviewing your constraints. Notes and caveats below; happy to walk through on the call.

1) CIDR and routing: we recommend reserving /24s per environment (prod/replica/poc). Example: HarborBank-prod: 10.10.32.0/24, HarborBank-repl: 10.10.33.0/24. Avoid overlapping with on-prem subnets to simplify peering and PrivateLink route tables.

2) PrivateLink limits: each interface endpoint has ENI bandwidth limits and scaling characteristics per cloud provider. For AWS, throughput per ENI can be tens to hundreds of Mbps depending on instance type of the service. For high TPS small-payload workloads (like RPC for inference), you’ll want multiple AZ-backed endpoints and client-side connection pooling. Test results attached show ~3–5ms median extra latency in-region for 1KB responses, 99th ~8–12ms depending on AZ placement.

3) VPC Peering pros/cons: NAT is not required if routing is configured; however, peering means you must manage route tables tightly to avoid accidental exposure. Peer-to-peer does not support transitive routing, so for cross-region or multi-VPC fabrics we prefer Transit Gateway as an orchestration plane. Transit Gateway adds cost but simplifies scaling/DR.

4) VPN notes: MTU and fragmentation issues are common with IPsec + UDP encapsulation; if you adopt VPN for on-prem, ensure MSS clamping on your edge devices. VPN is fine for low-volume control traffic, but not optimal for production inference without dedicated circuits (Direct Connect/ExpressRoute) or SD-WAN.

5) Observability/traceability: with PrivateLink you get clearer service boundaries (easier flow logs and per-endpoint security auditing). For peering, we'll rely on VPC flow logs + IDS.

I’ve attached a short checklist for the PoC and a small script we run to measure p95 latencies across AZs (see privatelink-performance-tests.xlsx).

—Connor

Anya / team — quick answers and proposed next steps. I’ve also uploaded a 1-page PoC SOW to the links above.

Cost (very rough):
- PrivateLink (multi-AZ, moderate throughput): initial infra + per-GB egress ~ moderate. Expect higher per-GB than peering but lower operational overhead and better isolation. For the scale you described (200–300 TPS of small payloads) budget ballpark: low-to-mid 10s of $k/month depending on AZ distribution and connection counts.
- Transit Gateway + peering (for replication fabric): higher flat monthly for TGW attachment + data transfer but better for large bulk replication traffic. TGW becomes more cost-effective if you have many VPCs or heavy cross-VPC data flows.

Latency: PrivateLink adds an extra hop (ENI -> service) — in-region medians are typically sub-ms to a few ms; p99 depends on AZ placement and backend load. Our tests show p99 in the 8–15ms range for small payloads at the scale you described; we'll include p99-focused tests in the PoC.

DNS / Certs: recommended approach for HarborBank: use your internal Private DNS (split-horizon) to point the service name to the interface endpoints, and Redwood will terminate TLS at the service but support end-to-end TLS when required. We can support customer-managed certs (uploaded to your KMS/HSM) or manage certs for the endpoint; CISO can choose. We support mTLS on the service side as an optional layer.

Proposed next steps:
1) Sign PoC SOW (I uploaded a draft: https://www.docusign.com/some-sow-link).
2) Schedule 45-min runbook + NetOps call (Wednesday 10:30 PT suggested).
3) Run PoC (2 weeks): deploy PrivateLink endpoints in 2 AZs, baseline throughput/latency, run p99 tests (we’ll provide the test harness), confirm routing and DNS.

If that works I’ll coordinate a short kickoff and include a checklist and SOW. Markus / Kimberly, can you support procurement and CISO outreach respectively?

Thanks — Olga
